transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-09-03
Start time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~67 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Ravi Desai (Cascade AI), Lina Morales (Infra Eng), Tom Wu (SRE)

Auto-generated summary: Covered trace/span model for token metrics, KV cache instrumentation, batching windows, and dashboard design. Agreed pilot and next steps.

Topics: OTLP collector config, token latency per-token, span naming, Grafana panels, VPC egress.

--- Transcript body (timestamps are periodic and approximate) ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're going to dig into how you can get token-level traces and metrics from Redwood's runtime into your observability stack. Jordan and I will walk through our recommended span model and an example collector config.
[00:18] Ravi Desai: Great, thanks. Our main ask is we need per-token latency breakdowns and also visibility into cache hits — our engineering team wants to see where KV cache is saving us and where it's not.
[00:28] Jordan Patel: Totally. High level, there are two streams: metrics (per-token latency histograms, token count, batching size) and traces (spans that mark cache hit/miss and batching windows). We prefer exporting both via OTLP to your collector.
[00:40] Lina Morales: Quick question — is it heavy to emit token-level metrics? We're worried about cardinality and cost.
[00:47] Jordan Patel: Good point. There are two patterns. 1) Emit summarized metrics per request: avg_latency_per_token, tokens_per_request, batch_size. 2) For debugging/pilot only, emit per-token traces — that is heavier. We usually recommend sampling those traces at 1-5% in production and 100% for the pilot.
[01:05] Tom Wu: When you say "per-token traces", do you mean a separate span for each token? That sounds like a lot.
[01:10] Jordan Patel: Yes — individual token spans are possible. In Redwood's runtime we create a lightweight child span for token generation when debug-level tracing is enabled. Span attributes include token_index, token_text (optional), latency_ms, kv_cache_hit (true/false), model_version, seq_len. But again, keep it sampled.
[01:27] Ravi Desai: Ok. For our dashboards we'd prefer token-level histograms (latency buckets) aggregated by model.version and by route.
[01:33] Maya Chen: That maps well. We advise using a histogram metric like redwood.token_latency_bucket with labels {model, variant, route, cache_hit, seq_len_bucket}. This gives you per-token histogram SLOs in Grafana.
[01:48] Jordan Patel: Also include a counter for cache hits and misses: redwood.kv_cache_hit_count and redwood.kv_cache_miss_count. You can compute hit rate in Prometheus/Grafana easily.
[01:58] Lina Morales: We're on-prem currently inside a VPC. How does the collector work with no egress?
[02:03] Maya Chen: You can run your OTLP collector inside the VPC and forward to your internal prometheus/grafana/tempo stack. For private Redwood deployments, we can also deploy a private collector that writes to your internal & optionally ships anonymized traces to Redwood for support under contracts.
[02:19] Tom Wu: What about metadata for trace grouping? We need to tag by customer_id and app_id.
[02:24] Jordan Patel: Resource attributes are the answer. Add resource attributes like deployment.environment, redwood.customer_id, redwood.app_id, model.name, model.variant. We recommend stable keys because they get attached to all spans and metrics.
[02:35] Ravi Desai: Can you show the span naming scheme you'd recommend?
[02:38] Jordan Patel: Sure. Example: span name = "redwood.generate.token" for individual token spans, parent span "redwood.generate.request" for the end-to-end request. Also add synthetic spans for "redwood.kvcache.lookup" with attribute hit=true/false and duration_ms. Batching windows can be a span named "redwood.batch.window" with attribute batch_size.
[02:58] Lina Morales: That helps. How do we correlate a cache lookup span to a specific token?
[03:02] Jordan Patel: Use traceparent / trace id — same trace for request and child spans. Also set attributes: token_index and maybe token_hash. Token_index is easiest.
[03:12] Ravi Desai: On the performance side, what overhead does this add? We can't accept large p95 regressions.
[03:18] Jordan Patel: In our measurements, emitting lightweight span events with attributes adds ~0.2-0.6ms per token when synchronous. If you async-batch spans to the collector or use a lower sampling rate, overhead drops to ~0.05-0.2ms. Quantization impacts token RT more heavily than tracing — a 4-bit quantized model can add up to 12-30% variance on cold starts depending on kernel availability.
[03:41] Tom Wu: You mentioned async-batching spans — is that the OTLP exporter doing batching?
[03:45] Jordan Patel: Yes — the collector SDK has exporters that buffer and send spans in batches. We recommend exporter settings: max_queue_size 5000, scheduled_delay_millis 500, max_export_batch_size 1024 for high-throughput workloads. That keeps CPU impact low and network efficient.
[04:02] Maya Chen: Also consider prefix/KV caching to reduce tokens emitted. If a request is served from prefix cache, you can add an attribute prefix_cache_hit=true and skip per-token emission — emit a single metric that the request was fully served from cache.
[04:16] Ravi Desai: Can you walk through a concrete dashboard layout? We currently use Grafana with Prometheus and Tempo.
[04:20] Jordan Patel: Panel suggestions: 1) Top-level KPIs — tokens/sec, avg latency per token (p50/p95/p99), cache hit rate. 2) Heatmap of latency by token position (token_index on X, latency on Y), 3) Batch size distribution over time, 4) Error rate and model fallbacks. 5) Trace sampling link — hover from a slow token to Tempo.
[04:43] Lina Morales: For the heatmap, would we store per-token histograms per model+route? That's a lot of series.
[04:48] Jordan Patel: Yes it's cardinality heavy. Two mitigations: bucket seq_len into ranges (0-32, 33-128, etc.) and only keep detailed per-token histograms for a rolling window (e.g., 24h). For long-term trends, store aggregated metrics.
[05:03] Tom Wu: Any advice about quantization and its visibility in metrics?
[05:06] Jordan Patel: Tag metrics with quantization_profile label (e.g., fp16, int8, q4_0). That lets you split latency by quantization. Also create synthetic metrics for cold_start_count per model.variant to see warmup behavior.
[05:18] Ravi Desai: We have a private deployment and want to correlate cost to tokens. Can we export token counts to billing systems?
[05:24] Maya Chen: You can export aggregated token counters (redwood.tokens_generated_total) to your billing pipeline. We also provide token attribution per route and per-customer in our usage exports if you want Redwood to send CSVs.
[05:35] Lina Morales: A few practical questions: 1) sample rate config in collector, 2) how to avoid PII in token_text attribute, 3) network egress encryption.
[05:42] Jordan Patel: 1) Sampling: set probabilistic sampling in the collector for spans (e.g., parent-based + trace-sampler with 0.01). For pilot, override to 1. 2) Token text: by default we recommend not sending token_text. If you need it for debugging, you can redaction-hook on our SDK or hash tokens before export. 3) OTLP over TLS to collector; for egress to Redwood we require mTLS and can accept collector connections from customer IP list when on-prem is used.
[06:10] Ravi Desai: Can you share an example otlp-collector config that shows resource attributes and sampling?
[06:14] Jordan Patel: Yes, we'll share the YAML after the call. It includes receivers: otlp, processors: batch, resource, tail_sampling, exporters: prometheus, tempo, and optional otlp/mtls backends. We'll include an example of resource detection and static attributes: redwood.customer_id and model.variant.
[06:27] Tom Wu: For the pilot, we want end-to-end: Redwood runtime -> local collector -> Tempo + Grafana, with traces sampled at 100% for 1000 requests. Does that make sense?
[06:35] Maya Chen: Yep, that's exactly the pilot we recommend. We can provide a small client workload script to generate requests and include a benchmark spreadsheet template.
[06:43] Ravi Desai: Are there any gotchas with batch windows? We noticed a few spikes in p95 correlated with large batch flushes.
[06:48] Jordan Patel: Large batch flushes can cause p99 spikes due to queueing latency — monitor batch_size percentiles. If you see large flushes, lower max_batch_latency_ms or configure dynamic batching thresholds. Also inspect if KV cache miss rate increases, because cache misses force extra model compute per token and can change batch behavior.
[07:07] Lina Morales: On the security side, we need to know what Redwood stores if we enable remote support.
[07:11] Maya Chen: For Redwood-managed support, we only request sampled traces and aggregated metrics. We have a SOC 2 summary and data retention controls; I'll share the link. Collectors can be configured to anonymize or hash attributes before export.
[07:21] Tom Wu: Do you have a suggested tagging scheme for multi-tenant dashboards?
[07:25] Jordan Patel: Use resource attributes: customer_id, org_unit, app_route, model.variant. Also add a stable service.name like redwood.inference.<env>. This helps you create templated dashboards in Grafana.
[07:36] Ravi Desai: Could you describe a realistic story: we see a p95 regression. How would we triage with your traces/metrics?
[07:42] Jordan Patel: Step 1: look at token-level histogram to find if early or late tokens are affected. Step 2: inspect batch_size distribution and batch.window spans. Step 3: look for kv_cache_miss_count spikes. Step 4: open a sampled trace for a slow request to see if the delay is in kernel selection, quantized ops, or network RPC. Add a flamegraph on compute step if available.
[08:05] Maya Chen: We'll attach a small checklist in the dashboard README: what panels to check first and which traces to pull.
[08:12] Ravi Desai: Great. A few small clarifications on implementation details?
[08:15] Tom Wu: Yeah, for exporter batching settings, is there guidance per instance size? Our nodes are 8xA100 and 4xA100 clusters.
[08:22] Jordan Patel: With A100s, throughput per GPU changes. For high throughput nodes, set max_export_batch_size to larger values (1024) and scheduled_delay lower (200-500ms). For smaller nodes, lower batch sizes to avoid memory pressure. We can share tuned defaults for common instance types in the YAML.
[08:40] Lina Morales: Regarding quantization labels — how granular should it be? q4_0 vs q4_1?
[08:44] Jordan Patel: Tag the quantization_profile as the exact identifier your model registry uses — that gives you precise filtering. If you want aggregated dashboards, create derived labels like quant_scheme (e.g., q4) while keeping the full profile for debugging.
[08:58] Ravi Desai: Are there any pre-built Grafana dashboards we can import?
[09:01] Maya Chen: Yes, Redwood has an observability dashboard pack we'll share. It includes panels for token histograms, batch diagnostics, cache heatmaps, and a trace drill-down link. We'll add a sample JSON to the shared drive.
[09:10] Jordan Patel: We'll also include a small Node/python client script that toggles debug tracing on a per-request header (X-Redwood-Trace: full) so you can run selective 100% trace windows.
[09:22] Ravi Desai: Perfect. One more question — how do you handle model rollouts? We need to compare new versus baseline.
[09:29] Jordan Patel: Add labels model.rollout_group and model.version on all metrics and spans. Then set Grafana panels to compare these groups. For automatic detection, Redwood can emit a metric redwood.version_switch_count when we flip routes.
[09:40] Lina Morales: Cool. Any notes on storage retention concerns? Tempo vs Jaeger vs hosted?
[09:45] Jordan Patel: Tempo is good for high-cardinality traces when used with long-term object storage. For pilot, 7-14 day retention is fine. If you need longer, consider flamegraph-level exports aggregated and store metrics instead of raw traces.
[09:58] Maya Chen: Ok, to recap: Jordan will share the collector YAML and dashboard JSON, Maya will share security docs and the dashboard pack, Cascade will run the 1k-request pilot and provide results, and Lina will provide VPC allowlist info.
[10:15] Ravi Desai: Sounds good. Anything else?
[10:18] Tom Wu: We've seen one more oddity — when using int8 quant on X model, the KV cache hit rate looks artificially low because prefixes are truncated. Is that something you've seen?
[10:27] Jordan Patel: Yes — certain quantization kernels may change tokenization boundaries subtly if custom tokenizers or merging heuristics are used. We recommend validating tokenization stable across quant variants and instrumenting a small token_equivalence_metric to detect divergence.
[10:41] Lina Morales: Noted. We'll look into tokenizer consistency.
[10:44] Maya Chen: We'll upload the checklist and the YAML right after. Links we'll provide: Redwood obs docs (https://redwood.example/docs/observability/otlp), shared dashboard pack (drive: https://drive.example.com/redwood-dashboard-pack), pilot benchmark template (https://drive.example.com/pilot-benchmark-template).
[10:59] Ravi Desai: Thanks everyone, this is helpful. We'll aim for the dates we discussed.
[11:03] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts and schedule the follow-up meeting for mid-September.

End of transcript.
